analysis.one_liner: Blocks any EPA limit on power plant carbon emissions until most other countries adopt equally strict rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Clean Air Act to stop any EPA rule limiting carbon dioxide emissions from coal- or gas-fired power plants from taking effect unless the EPA first certifies that other countries producing at least 80% of the world's carbon emissions (not counting the U.S.) have adopted equally strict rules. Because no such worldwide agreement exists, the practical effect would be to permanently block U.S. limits on power plant carbon pollution. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Environment Subcommittee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal-burning and gas-burning power plants and the coal, oil, and gas industries that supply them. With no federal limit on their carbon emissions allowed to take effect, they avoid the cost of controlling pollution from their plants.

how_it_helps.text: The bill forbids any EPA rule on carbon dioxide from fossil-fuel power plants from taking effect until the agency certifies that countries responsible for at least 80% of global carbon emissions (excluding the U.S.) have adopted regulations at least as strict, measured by numeric limits and timeframes [S2] [S3].

The bill text also states that nothing in it should be construed as giving the EPA any authority to issue regulations on, act on, or even consider carbon dioxide emissions, language that would foreclose future climate rules for power plants [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall on the public: more carbon pollution from power plants contributing to climate change, and the health effects of continued fossil-fuel combustion, while the plants that emit avoid compliance costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through pollution and climate damage

drawbacks.text: The certification condition is practically impossible to meet: it requires an estimated 80% of non-U.S. global carbon emissions to be covered by regulations exactly as strict in both numeric limit and timeframe, a standard no international climate arrangement has ever satisfied [S2] [S3].

Supporters of a condition like this argue the U.S. should not bear compliance costs while major emitters such as China and India do not; the bill's text frames the problem as 'unilateral' regulation [S3]. An honest supporter would acknowledge that under this bill, if other countries never match U.S. stringency, the U.S. simply never regulates power plant carbon emissions at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a fairness argument — that U.S. plants should not face costs while foreign competitors do not — but its actual mechanism does not level a playing field; it removes the possibility of U.S. limits altogether if the global standard is never met. The benefit accrues to polluting power plants and fuel suppliers; the cost, in pollution and climate risk, accrues to the public. The bill died without any committee action or vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Environment Subcommittee in May 2017 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended in January 2019 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Rothfus introduced the bill on May 16, 2017, with Reps. LaMalfa and McKinley as original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1] [S3] [S5].
Three days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment, where it remained; no further action was ever taken in the 115th Congress [S5].
The House adjourned for the last time on January 3, 2019, and all bills not enacted die at the end of a Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-fired power plants and the coal, oil, and gas industries are better off: no carbon limits on power plants were enacted in the 115th Congress, and this bill never advanced far enough to matter either way.

for.name: Rep. Keith Rothfus
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to condition any EPA power plant carbon rule on foreign adoption of equally strict rules.

for.name: Reps. Doug LaMalfa and David McKinley
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Environment and never scheduled a hearing or markup in the two years that followed.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had three Republican sponsors and no Democratic support appears in the record; no vote was ever taken, so no partisan split can be measured [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Coal mining and coal-fired electric power
industries.note: The bill would make it impossible for the EPA to limit carbon emissions from coal plants as long as the rest of the world does not adopt identical rules, sparing plants compliance costs while the public absorbs the pollution. Coal plants are the largest source of power-sector carbon emissions.
Gas plants, also covered by the prohibition on carbon rules, would avoid any compliance cost under the bill, with the health and climate cost shifted to the public.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and gas fuel suppliers
industries.note: With power-plant carbon regulation off the table, demand for fossil fuels in electricity generation would remain undisturbed.
